Indu: Heard about the Kochi hospital deal. Are you okay?
Nirmala: They signed with the other vendor. I wouldn't promise go-live by March.
Nirmala: We both know it's June at best.
Indu: You were right to say June.
Nirmala: Tell that to my target sheet. Feels like I'm the only one who thinks it mattered.
Indu: You're not. At stand-up I told the team exactly why we lost it.
Indu: Pooja said she'd have been the one fixing a broken launch in April.
Indu: And I've asked our lead to write the reason in your quarterly notes, not just the loss.
Nirmala: ...thanks. I nearly said March, you know. For about five seconds.
Indu: Five seconds is human. What you actually said is what counts 🤍
Nirmala: Chai at 4?
Indu: Already saved the corner table.

qa.q: Which go-live month did Nirmala refuse to promise?
qa.a: Nirmala wouldn't promise go-live by March, because it's June at best.

qa.q: How can you tell that Indu is worried about Nirmala?
qa.a: Indu feels concerned and protective; Indu messages first with "Are you okay?" and has already spoken up for Nirmala at stand-up.

qa.q: Which of Indu's steps would help most at review time, and why?
qa.a: Asking their lead to write the reason in the quarterly notes, so the record shows why the deal was lost and not just the loss.

qa.q: What is it like for Nirmala before and after hearing what Indu did?
qa.a: At first Nirmala feels alone, as if nobody else thought honesty mattered; after hearing about the team, Nirmala admits the five-second temptation and asks for chai 🙂

grounding: Shows a colleague noticing someone lose a deal for refusing to make a false promise, and backing them in front of the team so honesty is not carried alone.

The notice was pinned beside the collection window of the dairy cooperative: the new supervisor would be Deshmukh, not Anand. Varun read it twice while milk cans clanged behind him.
Everyone at the centre knew why. Before the district inspection, the secretary had asked Anand to "round up" the fat readings. Anand had written the real numbers and signed.
Now Anand sat at the testing bench, eyes on the machine, answering in single words.
At lunch Varun carried two steel tumblers of tea to the bench. "The farmers trust your register more than any notice," he said.
That evening, when the society met under the neem tree, Varun stood up. "Bhimrao-kaka's payment was right to the paisa because of Anand's readings." Two farmers nodded. Old Bhimrao came over and pressed Anand's shoulder.
Anand said little, but he stayed after the meeting and laughed once.

qa.q: Who was named the new supervisor on the notice?
qa.a: The new supervisor would be Deshmukh, not Anand.

qa.q: What was Varun feeling when carrying tea to the testing bench?
qa.a: Varun felt uneasy about the unfair notice and protective of Anand, wanting Anand to know the farmers trust the register.

qa.q: What could others at the centre do so Anand doesn't stand alone?
qa.a: Like Varun, they could say openly that Anand's honest readings protect the farmers' payments, and keep backing real numbers at the next inspection.

qa.q: How is Anand affected by what Varun said at the meeting?
qa.a: Anand had been answering in single words, but after the meeting he stayed back and laughed once, looking less alone.

grounding: Shows a worker at a village dairy centre noticing someone lose a promotion for refusing to falsify readings, and speaking up so that person is not left alone.

At the Nairobi office of the solar company, Wanjiru watched Ivan end the call with the big hotel chain. He had told them honestly that the panels couldn't arrive before March. A competitor had promised January. The hotel signed with them by lunch.
At the afternoon meeting the sales head said sharply, "We lost the biggest contract of the quarter because someone wanted to be a saint." Ivan stared at the table.
Wanjiru's heart was racing. She was new. But she said, "The January date wasn't possible. I checked the shipping schedule this morning. If we'd promised it, we'd have lost the client in March instead, and our name with it."
Two others nodded. After the meeting a senior engineer bought Ivan a coffee.
Three months later the hotel chain called back. The competitor's panels hadn't arrived. They asked for Ivan by name.

qa.q: When could the panels actually arrive?
qa.a: Not before March.

qa.q: What was Wanjiru feeling before speaking up in the meeting?
qa.a: Wanjiru's heart was racing; Wanjiru felt nervous as a newcomer but moved to defend Ivan.

qa.q: How did Wanjiru support Ivan in a way that helped?
qa.a: She backed his honesty with a fact, the shipping schedule, in front of the team, which led others to show support too.

qa.q: What was the afternoon meeting like for Ivan?
qa.a: Ivan was publicly mocked as a saint for losing the contract and stared at the table, likely feeling ashamed and alone until Wanjiru spoke.

grounding: Shows a new colleague publicly backing a teammate who lost a deal by refusing to promise a false date, so his honesty was not a lonely choice.

In the nurses' station of the district hospital, the promotion list went up on Monday. Pallavi's name wasn't on it. Everyone knew why: in March she had refused to sign the infection-control checklist for a ward she hadn't inspected, and the matron had called her "difficult" ever since.
Asif had seen it happen. He had signed his own checklist that day without checking, and he hadn't slept well since.
Pallavi read the list, smiled tightly, and went back to changing a dressing.
At tea Asif said to the others, loud enough for her to hear, "Pallavi's checks are the only ones I trust on this floor. That's why I asked her to look over my ward today." A couple of nurses murmured agreement.
Then he did the harder thing. He went to the nursing superintendent and said his March checklist had been signed without an inspection, and that Pallavi's refusal had been right.
That evening Pallavi left a vada on his desk, wrapped in a napkin.

qa.q: What had Pallavi refused to sign in March?
qa.a: The infection-control checklist for a ward she hadn't inspected.

qa.q: What had Asif been feeling since March?
qa.a: Asif felt guilty and hadn't slept well, having signed his own checklist without checking.

qa.q: Which two things did Asif do to support Pallavi?
qa.a: He praised her checks openly at tea, and told the nursing superintendent that his March checklist was signed without an inspection and that Pallavi was right.

qa.q: What might the promotion list have been like for Pallavi?
qa.a: Pallavi was likely hurt and disappointed, smiling tightly, paying for her honesty while others moved ahead.

grounding: Shows a nurse recognising and backing a colleague who lost a promotion for refusing to sign a false checklist, and correcting his own record.

subtype: Honouring a colleague who pays the price [Observer]
passage:
Dear Preeti,
I wanted to put this in writing, because saying it in the corridor felt too small.
Last week, when the director asked you to tell the client our face cream was "clinically proven", you said no, because there was no trial. You said you'd rather lose the account than put your name to that. We lost the account. I watched your face when the director said, "Some people aren't team players."
I said nothing in that room. I'm sorry. I should have.
So here's what I've done since: I told the director that I agree with you, and that I won't write that claim either. Three of us from the copy team have signed a short note asking for proof before any "proven" claim goes out.
You're not alone in this. You shouldn't have been, even for a week.
Kalyani

qa.q: What did the director want Preeti to tell the client?
qa.a: That the face cream was 'clinically proven'.

qa.q: How does Kalyani feel about staying silent in the room?
qa.a: Kalyani feels sorry and ashamed about saying nothing, which is why this letter and the note followed.

qa.q: How did Kalyani turn regret into support?
qa.a: By telling the director Kalyani agrees with Preeti, refusing to write the claim, and getting three copywriters to sign a note asking for proof.

qa.q: What might that week have been like for Preeti?
qa.a: Preeti lost the account and was called not a team player, likely feeling isolated until colleagues stood alongside Preeti.

grounding: Shows a colleague who first stayed silent then openly backing a coworker who lost an account for refusing to make a false claim.

subtype: Honouring a colleague who pays the price [Observer]

You asked why I keep backing Payal in meetings. Here's the story, and yes, it's me, Tarun, the one who stayed quiet at first.

Last quarter our biggest client wanted us to confirm the software had passed its security audit. It hadn't finished. Our manager said, "Just tell them it's done."

Payal said no, calmly. "I can tell them the date it will be done."

The client went elsewhere. In March the team-lead post went to someone else, and everyone knew why.

For a week she ate lunch alone at her desk. I kept thinking she must feel like the only fool in the building, and that the rest of us had let her be one.

So I took my lunch to her desk. In the review meeting I said out loud that she had kept us from a false claim. Two others backed me.

It didn't get her the post. But she told me the lunches mattered more than she expected, and it has changed how I'll answer the next time someone asks me to fudge something.

qa.q: What did Payal offer to tell the client instead?
qa.a: Payal said she could tell them the date it will be done.

qa.q: What did Tarun feel while watching Payal eat lunch alone?
qa.a: Tarun felt uneasy and guilty, imagining she must feel like the only fool in the building and that the others, Tarun included, had let her be one.

qa.q: How could colleagues support someone who pays a price for honesty?
qa.a: Sit with them, say publicly what their honesty protected the team from, and back them in meetings, so they are not left standing alone.

qa.q: What was it like for Payal when colleagues backed her in the review meeting?
qa.a: Payal felt less isolated; she later said the lunches mattered more than she expected, even though the post still went to someone else.

grounding: Illustrates a colleague who watches a teammate lose a client and a promotion for refusing to lie, and supports her openly so honesty is not a lonely choice.
